traps.excerpt: P06 was subjected entirely to leading questions, making the interview methodologically invalid [P06:t1, P06:t2, P06:t8].
P07 is a solo university student who cooks once a week and relies on takeout, outside the target definition [P07, P07:t1].
P09 represents a retired couple who have maintained the same cooking routine for forty years with zero desire for digital tools [P09, P09:t1].

P08 claimed an extreme willingness to pay EUR 30 a month after throwing out EUR 200 of spoiled holiday food, but this represents an unvalidated extreme stated preference following a one-off trauma [P08:t2, P08:t9].
Inventory onboarding friction risk: If users are forced to scan or type pantry contents manually, they will churn immediately [P02:t8, P05:t8, P08:t8, P10:t8].

One participant stated, "Planning is my favourite part of the week, honestly. I would never want an app to take that away from me." [P03:t1]. Another stated, "Planning ahead stresses me out. A plan I don't follow feels like failure, so I decide on the day." [P05:t1].
Household sync risk: Uncoordinated shopping by multiple partners creates waste and duplicates unless updates sync in real time [P02:t2, P04:t4, P10:t2].

Claim that 97% of households would pay for automated meal planning: This figure from App Trends Blog is an extreme outlier contradicted by interview data where most users seek free or low-cost apps [P01:t9, P02:t9, P03:t9, P05:t9, S08]. Claim that the meal-planning market grows by 25% annually: Snippet S06 lists no source and no year, making it unverified [S06]. Claim that 73% of families struggle with dinner decisions: Snippet S07 provides no source and no year, making it unverified [S07]. Claim that online grocery purchases represent only 4%: Snippet S09 comes from a 2016 study, which is a decade old and likely outdated [S09].

criteria.justification: The brief is highly comprehensive and answers all six required questions with rich detail, successfully linking problems to specific customer segments and market data.
Every key claim is tightly grounded in explicitly cited sources. The brief actively distinguishes between actual behaviors and stated preferences, maximizing the clarity of the evidence.

The brief is generally well-calibrated, identifying invalid interviews and rejecting extreme outlier figures. However, it fails to recognize identical templated responses from participants as an anomaly, mistakenly treating them as independent verification.

The recommendations are clear and tightly mapped to the riskiest assumptions. The proposed experiments are exceptionally concrete, fully detailing the target audience, method, sample sizes, and threshold success metrics.
The brief is perfectly concise and highly readable. It uses strong structural formatting like bullet points and bold headers, making it completely effortless for a product team to scan and act upon.
